# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# similar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/similar/^2/

## Expand description

This crate implements diffing utilities. It attempts to provide an abstraction interface over different types of diffing algorithms. The design of the library is inspired by pijul’s diff library by Pierre-Étienne Meunier and also inherits the patience diff algorithm from there.

The API of the crate is split into high and low level functionality. Most of what you probably want to use is available top level. Additionally the following sub modules exist:

- `algorithms`
- `udiff`
- `utils`

[§](https://docs.rs#sequence-diffing)Sequence Diffing

If you want to diff sequences generally indexable things you can use the
[ capture_diff](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff.html) and

[functions. They will directly diff an indexable object or slice and return a vector of](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices.html)

`capture_diff_slices`[objects.](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html)

`DiffOp````
use similar::{Algorithm, capture_diff_slices};
let a = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let b = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 7];
let ops = capture_diff_slices(Algorithm::Myers, &a, &b);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#text-diffing)Text Diffing

Similar provides helpful utilities for text (and more specifically line) diff
operations.  The main type you want to work with is [ TextDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html) which
uses the underlying diff algorithms to expose a convenient API to work with
texts:

```
use similar::{ChangeTag, TextDiff};
let diff = TextDiff::from_lines(
    "Hello World\nThis is the second line.\nThis is the third.",
    "Hallo Welt\nThis is the second line.\nThis is life.\nMoar and more",
);
for change in diff.iter_all_changes() {
    let sign = match change.tag() {
        ChangeTag::Delete => "-",
        ChangeTag::Insert => "+",
        ChangeTag::Equal => " ",
    };
    print!("{}{}", sign, change);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#trailing-newlines)Trailing Newlines

When working with line diffs (and unified diffs in general) there are two
“philosophies” to look at lines.  One is to diff lines without their newline
character, the other is to diff with the newline character.  Typically the
latter is done because text files do not *have* to end in a newline character.
As a result there is a difference between `foo\n` and `foo` as far as diffs
are concerned.

In similar this is handled on the [ Change](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html) or

[level. If a diff was created via](https://docs.rs/struct.InlineChange.html)

`InlineChange`[the text diffing system is instructed to check if there are missing newlines encountered (](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.from_lines)

`TextDiff::from_lines`[returns true).](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.newline_terminated)

`TextDiff::newline_terminated`In any case the [ Change](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html) object has a convenience method called

[which returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html#method.missing_newline)

`Change::missing_newline``true` if the change is missing
a trailing newline.  Armed with that information the caller knows to handle
this by either rendering a virtual newline at that position or to indicate
it in different ways.  For instance the unified diff code will render the
special `\ No newline at end of file` marker.[§](https://docs.rs#bytes-vs-unicode)Bytes vs Unicode

Similar module concerns itself with a looser definition of “text” than you would
normally see in Rust.  While by default it can only operate on [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) types,
by enabling the

`bytes` feature it gains support for byte slices with some
caveats.A lot of text diff functionality assumes that what is being diffed constitutes text, but in the real world it can often be challenging to ensure that this is all valid utf-8. Because of this the crate is built so that most functionality also still works with bytes for as long as they are roughly ASCII compatible.

This means you will be successful in creating a unified diff from latin1 encoded bytes but if you try to do the same with EBCDIC encoded bytes you will only get garbage.

[§](https://docs.rs#ops-vs-changes)Ops vs Changes

Because very commonly two compared sequences will largely match this module splits its functionality into two layers:

Changes are encoded as [diff operations](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html).  These are
ranges of the differences by index in the source sequence.  Because this
can be cumbersome to work with, a separate method [ DiffOp::iter_changes](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html#method.iter_changes)
(and

[when working with text diffs) is provided which expands all the changes on an item by item level encoded in an operation.](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.iter_changes)

`TextDiff::iter_changes`As the [ TextDiff::grouped_ops](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.grouped_ops) method can isolate clusters of changes
this even works for very long files if paired with this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#deadlines-and-performance)Deadlines and Performance

For large and very distinct inputs the algorithms as implemented can take
a very, very long time to execute.  Too long to make sense in practice.
To work around this issue all diffing algorithms also provide a version
that accepts a deadline which is the point in time as defined by an
[ Instant](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html) after which the algorithm should give up.  What giving up means
depends on the algorithm.  For instance due to the recursive, divide and
conquer nature of Myer’s diff you will still get a pretty decent diff in
many cases when a deadline is reached.  Whereas on the other hand the LCS
diff is unlikely to give any decent results in such a situation.

The [ TextDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html) type also lets you configure a deadline and/or timeout
when performing a text diff.

Note that on wasm targets calling [ Instant::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html#method.now) will result in a panic
unless you enable the

`wasm32_web_time` feataure.  By default similar will
silently disable the deadline checks internally unless that feature is
enabled.[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

The crate by default does not have any dependencies however for some use cases it’s useful to pull in extra functionality. Likewise you can turn off some functionality.

- `text`: this feature is enabled by default and enables the text based diffing types such as- `TextDiff`
- `unicode`: when this feature is enabled the text diffing functionality gains the ability to diff on a grapheme instead of character level. This is particularly useful when working with text containing emojis. This pulls in some relatively complex dependencies for working with the unicode database.
- `bytes`: this feature adds support for working with byte slices in text APIs in addition to unicode strings. This pulls in the- `bstr`
- `inline`: this feature gives access to additional functionality of the text diffing to provide inline information about which values changed in a line diff. This currently also enables the- `unicode`feature.
- `serde`: this feature enables serialization to some types in this crate. For enums without payload deserialization is then also supported.
- `wasm32_web_time`: this feature swaps out the use of- `std::time`- `web_time`crate. Because this is a change to the public interface, this feature must be used with care. The instant type for this crate is then re-exported top-level module.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [algorithms](https://docs.rs/algorithms/index.html)
- Various diff (longest common subsequence) algorithms.
- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- The various iterators this crate provides.
- [udiff](https://docs.rs/udiff/index.html)
- This module provides unified diff functionality.
- [utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)
- Utilities for common diff related operations.

- Represents the expanded `DiffOp`
- [Inline](https://docs.rs/struct.InlineChange.html)- Change
- Represents the expanded textual change with inline highlights.
- [Instant](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html)
- WASM (browser) specific instant type.
- [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html)- Diff

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Change](https://docs.rs/enum.ChangeTag.html)- Tag
- The tag of a change.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff.html)- diff
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_deadline.html)- diff_ - deadline
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices.html)- diff_ - slices
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices_deadline.html)- diff_ - slices_ - deadline
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_close_matches.html)- close_ - matches
- Use the text differ to find `n`close matches.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_diff_ratio.html)- diff_ - ratio
- Return a measure of similarity in the range `0..=1`.
- [group_](https://docs.rs/fn.group_diff_ops.html)- diff_ - ops
- Isolate change clusters by eliminating ranges with no changes.

# wayland_scanner - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-scanner/0.31.10/target-redirect/wayland_scanner/

## Expand description

Wayland protocol code-generation machinnery

This crate provides procedural macros for generating the rust code associated with a
Wayland XML protocol specification, for use with the `wayland-client`, `wayland-server`
and `wayland-backend` crates.

Before trying to use this crate, you may check if the protocol extension you want to use
is not already exposed in the `wayland-protocols` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-usage)Example usage

Below is a template for generating the code for a custom protocol client-side. Server-side
is identical, just replacing `client` by `server`. The path to the XML file is relative to the
crate root.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Generate the bindings in their own module
pub mod my_protocol {
    use wayland_client;
    // import objects from the core protocol if needed
    use wayland_client::protocol::*;
    // This module hosts a low-level representation of the protocol objects
    // you will not need to interact with it yourself, but the code generated
    // by the generate_client_code! macro will use it
    pub mod __interfaces {
        // import the interfaces from the core protocol if needed
        use wayland_client::protocol::__interfaces::*;
        wayland_scanner::generate_interfaces!("./path/to/the/protocol.xml");
    }
    use self::__interfaces::*;
    // This macro generates the actual types that represent the wayland objects of
    // your custom protocol
    wayland_scanner::generate_client_code!("./path/to/the/protocol.xml");
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_client_code.html)- client_ - code
- Proc-macro for generating client-side API associated with an XML specification
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_interfaces.html)- interfaces
- Proc-macro for generating low-level interfaces associated with an XML specification
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_server_code.html)- server_ - code
- Proc-macro for generating server-side API associated with an XML specification

---

# wayland-server 0.31.13 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-server/0.31.13

# wayland-server

Server side API for the Wayland protocol. This crate provides infrastructure for manipulating
Wayland objects, as well as object definitions for the core Wayland protocol. Protocol extensions
can be supported as well by combining this crate with `wayland-protocols`, which provides object
definitions for a large set of extensions.

**Note:** This crate is a low-level interface to the Wayland protocol. If you are looking for a more
battery-included toolkit for writing a Wayland server, you may consider
[Smithay](https://github.com/Smithay/smithay), which is a Wayland server framework built on top of it.

The crate has different backends to Wayland protocol serialization:

- By default, it uses a pure-rust implementation of the protocol, and contains little `unsafe`code.
- Activating the `use_system_lib`makes it instead bind to the system`libwayland-server.so`. This allows you to access C pointer versions of the wayland objects, which is necessary for interfacing with other non-Rust Wayland-related libraries (such as for OpenGL support, see the`wayland-egl`crate).
- Activating the `dlopen`implies`use_system_lib`, but additionaly the crate will not explicitly link to`libwayland-server.so`and instead try to open it at runtime, and return an error if it cannot find it. This allows you to build apps that can gracefully run in non-Wayland environment without needing compile-time switches.

---

# wayland-server 0.31.13 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-server/0.31.13/source/

#
                    wayland-server 0.31.13

# wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-server/0.31.13/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/wayland_server/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, server-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) and

[structs, resources (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)

`Resource`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) is the heart of this crate, it represents the protocol state of your Wayland server, and
takes care of processing messages from clients. You’ll need to integrate it in your event loop (see its
documentation for details). From it you can retrieve the

[, which is a clonable handle to the Wayland state and is the type used to actually interact with the protocol.](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`Each of the Wayland object you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)
trait. Thos structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.The request dispatching logic provided by this crate is build around the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait. During the
dispatching process (in

[), all requests sent by clients are read from their respective process and delivered to your processing logic, by invoking methods on the various](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html#method.dispatch_clients)

`Display::dispatch_clients()`[implementations of your](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``State` struct. In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement
`Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to process events for.However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse on your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#globals)Globals

The entry point of the protocol for clients goes through the protocol globals. Each global represents a
capability of your compositor, a peripheral it has access to, or a protocol extension it supports.
Globals are created by you using [ DisplayHandle::create_global()](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html#method.create_global), and require your

`State` to
implement the [trait for the interface associated with that global.](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)

`GlobalDispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

This crate can generate some runtime error message (notably when a protocol error occurs). By default
those messages are printed to stderr. If you activate the `log` cargo feature, they will instead be
piped through the `log` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait is impractical. In
those contexts, this crate also provides some escape-hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from

`wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects by directly providing
implementations of the backend [trait. See](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.create_resource_from_objdata)

`Client::create_resource_from_objdata()`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html#method.custom_init)

`DataInit::custom_init()`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI, such as for example when interfacing with the graphics stack for enabling hardware acceleration for clients.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

Then, you’ll generally need:

- The `*mut wl_display`pointer, that you can retrieve by first retrieving the`Backend``Display::backend()``.handle()``.display_ptr()`
- The `*mut wl_resource`pointers for the objects you need to share, by first getting the`ObjectId``Resource::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

If you need to receive pointers from FFI, you can make [ ObjectId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html)s from the

`*mut wl_resource` pointers
using [, and then make the resources using](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html#method.from_ptr)

`ObjectId::from_ptr()`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#tymethod.from_id)

`Resource::from_id()`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [delegate_](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html)- dispatch
- A helper macro which delegates a set of `Dispatch``Dispatch`
- [delegate_](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_global_dispatch.html)- global_ - dispatch
- A helper macro which delegates a set of `GlobalDispatch``GlobalDispatch`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A struct representing a Wayland client connected to your compositor.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)- Init
- Helper to initialize client-created objects
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- The Wayland display
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle to the Wayland display
- [Listening](https://docs.rs/struct.ListeningSocket.html)- Socket
- An utility representing a unix socket on which your compositor is listening for new clients
- [New](https://docs.rs/struct.New.html)
- A newly created object that needs to be initialized. See `DataInit`
- [Resource](https://docs.rs/struct.ResourceData.html)- Data
- The `ObjectData`
- [Weak](https://docs.rs/struct.Weak.html)
- A weak handle to a Wayland object

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Bind](https://docs.rs/enum.BindError.html)- Error
- Error that can occur when trying to bind a `ListeningSocket`
- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/enum.DispatchError.html)- Error
- An error generated if an illegal request was received from a client
- [WEnum](https://docs.rs/enum.WEnum.html)
- An enum value in the protocol.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)
- A trait which provides an implementation for handling a client’s requests from a resource with some type of associated user data.
- [Global](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)- Dispatch
- A trait which provides an implementation for handling advertisement of a global to clients with some type of associated user data.
- [Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)
- Trait representing a Wayland interface

`Resource::from_id()`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [delegate_](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html)- dispatch

# wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-server/0.31.13/target-redirect/wayland_server/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, server-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) and

[structs, resources (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)

`Resource`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) is the heart of this crate, it represents the protocol state of your Wayland server, and
takes care of processing messages from clients. You’ll need to integrate it in your event loop (see its
documentation for details). From it you can retrieve the

[, which is a clonable handle to the Wayland state and is the type used to actually interact with the protocol.](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`Each of the Wayland object you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)
trait. Thos structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.The request dispatching logic provided by this crate is build around the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait. During the
dispatching process (in

[), all requests sent by clients are read from their respective process and delivered to your processing logic, by invoking methods on the various](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html#method.dispatch_clients)

`Display::dispatch_clients()`[implementations of your](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``State` struct. In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement
`Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to process events for.However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse on your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#globals)Globals

The entry point of the protocol for clients goes through the protocol globals. Each global represents a
capability of your compositor, a peripheral it has access to, or a protocol extension it supports.
Globals are created by you using [ DisplayHandle::create_global()](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html#method.create_global), and require your

`State` to
implement the [trait for the interface associated with that global.](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)

`GlobalDispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

This crate can generate some runtime error message (notably when a protocol error occurs). By default
those messages are printed to stderr. If you activate the `log` cargo feature, they will instead be
piped through the `log` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait is impractical. In
those contexts, this crate also provides some escape-hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from

`wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects by directly providing
implementations of the backend [trait. See](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.create_resource_from_objdata)

`Client::create_resource_from_objdata()`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html#method.custom_init)

`DataInit::custom_init()`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI, such as for example when interfacing with the graphics stack for enabling hardware acceleration for clients.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

Then, you’ll generally need:

- The `*mut wl_display`pointer, that you can retrieve by first retrieving the`Backend``Display::backend()``.handle()``.display_ptr()`
- The `*mut wl_resource`pointers for the objects you need to share, by first getting the`ObjectId``Resource::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

If you need to receive pointers from FFI, you can make [ ObjectId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html)s from the

`*mut wl_resource` pointers
using [, and then make the resources using](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html#method.from_ptr)

`ObjectId::from_ptr()`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#tymethod.from_id)

`Resource::from_id()`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# Display in wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/struct.Display.html

`pub struct Display<State: 'static> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Wayland display

This struct is the core of your Wayland compositor. You’ll use it in your event loop to drive the
protocol processing of all your clients. All other interactions with the protocol itself are done
through the [ DisplayHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html) struct, on which the

`State` type parameter is erased for convenience.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The main loop of a Wayland compositor generally needs to wait on several sources of events, using
tools like `epoll` (on Linux). The Wayland display can be integrated in this mechanism by getting the
file descriptor as from `.backend()`[ .poll_fd()](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.Backend.html#method.poll_fd) and invoking
the

[method whenever it becomes readable.](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html#method.dispatch_clients)

`dispatch_clients()`To ensure all clients receive the events your compositor sends them, you also need to regularly invoke
the [ flush_clients()](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html#method.flush_clients) method, which will write the outgoing buffers into the
sockets.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new Wayland display

Can only fail if both the `server_system` and `dlopen` features of `wayland-backend` were enabled,
and the `libwayland-server.so` library could not be found.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#58-60)

Dispatch all requests received from clients to their respective callbacks.

The `state` argument is the main state of your compositor, which will be accessible from most of your
callbacks.

This client will be associated with the provided [ ClientData](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ClientData.html), that you can then retrieve from
it via

`Display`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#126-139)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#126-139)

Create a new protocol global

This global will be advertized to clients through the `wl_registry` according to the rules
defined by your [ GlobalDispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html) implementation for the given interface. Whenever a client
binds this global, the associated

[method will be invoked on your](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html#tymethod.bind)

`GlobalDispatch::bind()``State`.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#146-148)#### pub fn [disable_global](https://docs.rs#method.disable_global)<State: 'static>(&self, id: [GlobalId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.GlobalId.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#146-148)

#### pub fn [disable_global](https://docs.rs#method.disable_global)<State: 'static>(&self, id: [GlobalId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.GlobalId.html))

Disable this global

Clients will be notified of the global removal, and it will not be advertized to new clients. However the state associated with this global is not freed, so clients which already know about it can still bind it.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#160-162)#### pub fn [remove_global](https://docs.rs#method.remove_global)<State: 'static>(&self, id: [GlobalId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.GlobalId.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/display.rs.html#160-162)

#### pub fn [remove_global](https://docs.rs#method.remove_global)<State: 'static>(&self, id: [GlobalId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.GlobalId.html))

Remove this global

Clients will be notified of the global removal if it was not already disabled. The state associated with this global is freed, meaning clients trying to bind it will receive a protocol error.

When removing a global, it is recommended to first disable it using
[ disable_global()](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html#method.disable_global) to allow some time for clients to register that
the global is getting removed, to avoid a race where a client would be killed because it bound a global
at the same as the server decided to remove it. After the global has been disabled for some time (like
a few seconds) it should be safe to actually remove it.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Checks if the Wayland object associated with this proxy is still alive

Trigger a protocol error on this object

The `code` is intended to be from the `Error` enum declared alongside that object interface.

A protocol error is fatal to the Wayland connection, and the client will be disconnected.

Creates a weak handle to this object

This weak handle will not keep the user-data associated with the object alive,
and can be converted back to a full resource using [ Weak::upgrade()](https://docs.rs/struct.Weak.html#method.upgrade).

This can be of use if you need to store resources in the used data of other objects and want to be sure to avoid reference cycles that would cause memory leaks.

# Dispatch in wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/trait.Dispatch.html

`pub trait Dispatch<I: `[Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html), UserData, State = Self>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [request](https://docs.rs#tymethod.request)(
        state: [&mut State](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
        client: &[Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html),
        resource: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
        request: I::[Request](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#associatedtype.Request),
        data: [&UserData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
        dhandle: &[DisplayHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html),
        data_init: &mut [DataInit](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)<'_, State>,
    );
    // Provided method
    fn [destroyed](https://docs.rs#method.destroyed)(
        _state: [&mut State](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
        _client: [ClientId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ClientId.html),
        _resource: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
        _data: [&UserData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    ) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait which provides an implementation for handling a client’s requests from a resource with some type of associated user data.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-usage)General usage

You need to implement this trait on your `State` for every type of Wayland object that will be processed
by the [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) working with your

`State`.You can have different implementations of the trait for the same interface but different `UserData` type,
this way the events for a given object will be processed by the adequate implementation depending on
which `UserData` was assigned to it at creation.

The way this trait works is that the [ Dispatch::request()](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html#tymethod.request) method will be invoked by the

[for every request received by an object. Your implementation can then match on the associated](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)

`Display`[enum and do any processing needed with that event.](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#associatedtype.Request)

`Resource::Request`If the request being processed created a new object, you’ll receive it as a [ New<I>](https://docs.rs/struct.New.html). When that is the
case, you

*must*initialize it using the

[argument. **Failing to do so will cause a](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)

`DataInit`**panic**.

[§](https://docs.rs#modularity)Modularity

To provide generic handlers for downstream usage, it is possible to make an implementation of the trait
that is generic over the last type argument, as illustrated below. Users will then be able to
automatically delegate their implementation to yours using the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro.

As a result, when your implementation is instanciated, the last type parameter `State` will be the state
struct of the app using your generic implementation. You can put additional trait constraints on it to
specify an interface between your module and downstream code, as illustrated in this example:

```
use wayland_server::{protocol::wl_output, Dispatch};
/// The type we want to delegate to
struct DelegateToMe;
/// The user data relevant for your implementation.
/// When providing delegate implementation, it is recommended to use your own type here, even if it is
/// just a unit struct: using () would cause a risk of clashing with an other such implementation.
struct MyUserData;
// Now a generic implementation of Dispatch, we are generic over the last type argument instead of using
// the default State=Self.
impl<State> Dispatch<wl_output::WlOutput, MyUserData, State> for DelegateToMe
where
    // State is the type which has delegated to this type, so it needs to have an impl of Dispatch itself
    State: Dispatch<wl_output::WlOutput, MyUserData>,
    // If your delegate type has some internal state, it'll need to access it, and you can
    // require it by adding custom trait bounds.
    // In this example, we just require an AsMut implementation
    State: AsMut<DelegateToMe>,
{
    fn request(
        state: &mut State,
        _client: &wayland_server::Client,
        _resource: &wl_output::WlOutput,
        _request: wl_output::Request,
        _udata: &MyUserData,
        _dhandle: &wayland_server::DisplayHandle,
        _data_init: &mut wayland_server::DataInit<'_, State>,
    ) {
        // Here the delegate may handle incoming requests as it pleases.
        // For example, it retrives its state and does some processing with it
        let me: &mut DelegateToMe = state.as_mut();
        // do something with `me` ...
    }
}
```
**Note:** Due to limitations in Rust’s trait resolution algorithm, a type providing a generic
implementation of [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) cannot be used directly as the dispatching state, as rustc
currently fails to understand that it also provides

`Dispatch<I, U, Self>` (assuming all other
trait bounds are respected as well).## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/dispatch.rs.html#95-103)#### fn [request](https://docs.rs#tymethod.request)(
    state: [&mut State](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    client: &[Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html),
    resource: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    request: I::[Request](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#associatedtype.Request),
    data: [&UserData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    dhandle: &[DisplayHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html),
    data_init: &mut [DataInit](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)<'_, State>,
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/dispatch.rs.html#95-103)

#### fn [request](https://docs.rs#tymethod.request)(
    state: [&mut State](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    client: &[Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html),
    resource: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    request: I::[Request](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#associatedtype.Request),
    data: [&UserData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    dhandle: &[DisplayHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html),
    data_init: &mut [DataInit](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)<'_, State>,
)

Called when a request from a client is processed.

The implementation of this function will vary depending on what protocol is being implemented. Typically the server may respond to clients by sending events to the resource, or some other resource stored in the user data.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Called when the object this user data is associated with has been destroyed.

Note this type only provides an immutable reference to the user data, you will need to use interior mutability to change it.

Typically a [ Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html) would be used to have interior mutability.

You are given the [ ObjectId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html) and

[associated with the destroyed object for cleanup convenience.](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ClientId.html)

`ClientId`By default this method does nothing.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# delegate_dispatch in wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/macro.delegate_dispatch.html

```
macro_rules! delegate_dispatch {
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $dispatch_from:ty : [$interface: ty: $udata: ty] => $dispatch_to: ty) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A helper macro which delegates a set of [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) implementations for a resource to some other type which
provides a generic

[implementation.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`This macro allows more easily delegating smaller parts of the protocol a compositor may wish to handle in a modular fashion.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

For example, say you want to delegate events for [ WlOutput](https://docs.rs/protocol/wl_output/struct.WlOutput.html)
to the

`DelegateToMe` type from the [documentation.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch````
use wayland_server::{delegate_dispatch, protocol::wl_output};
// ExampleApp is the type events will be dispatched to.
/// The application state
struct ExampleApp {
    /// The delegate for handling wl_registry events.
    delegate: DelegateToMe,
}
// Use delegate_dispatch to implement Dispatch<wl_output::WlOutput, MyUserData> for ExampleApp.
delegate_dispatch!(ExampleApp: [wl_output::WlOutput: MyUserData] => DelegateToMe);
// DelegateToMe requires that ExampleApp implements AsMut<DelegateToMe>, so we provide the trait implementation.
impl AsMut<DelegateToMe> for ExampleApp {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut DelegateToMe {
        &mut self.delegate
    }
}
```

---

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/global.rs.html#119-121)

#### fn [can_view](https://docs.rs#method.can_view)(_client: [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html), _global_data: [&GlobalData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Checks if the global should be advertised to some client.

The implementation of this function determines whether a client may see and bind some global. If this function returns false, the client will not be told the global exists and attempts to bind the global will raise a protocol error.

One use of this function is implementing privileged protocols such as XWayland keyboard grabbing which must only be used by XWayland.

The default implementation allows all clients to see the global.

corresponding object is not of the interface `I`.

# DataInit in wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/struct.DataInit.html

`pub struct DataInit<'a, D: 'static> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Helper to initialize client-created objects

This helper is provided to you in your [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) and

[to initialize objects created by the client, by assigning them their user-data (or](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)

`GlobalDispatch`[if you need to go this lower-level route).](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`This step is mandatory, and **failing to initialize a newly created object will cause a panic**.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/dispatch.rs.html#163-176)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_server/dispatch.rs.html#163-176)

Initialize an object by assigning it its user-data

Set a custom [ ObjectData](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html) for this object

This object data is not managed by `wayland-server`, as a result you will not
be able to retreive it through [ Resource::data()](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#tymethod.data).
Instead, you’ll need to retrieve it using

[and handle the downcasting yourself.](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#tymethod.object_data)

# delegate_global_dispatch in wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/macro.delegate_global_dispatch.html

```
macro_rules! delegate_global_dispatch {
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $dispatch_from:ty : [$interface: ty: $udata: ty] => $dispatch_to: ty) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A helper macro which delegates a set of [ GlobalDispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html) implementations for a resource to some other type which
provdes a generic

[implementation.](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)

`GlobalDispatch`Its usage is similar to the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro.
